clinicalPearls: Germline activating (gain-of-function) variants in STAT3 cause early-onset, multi-organ autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, the mechanistic mirror image of STAT3 loss-of-function, which produces autosomal dominant hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome.
Typical presentation is an infant or young child with combinations of autoimmune cytopenias, enteropathy with failure to thrive, early-onset type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.
Short stature and growth failure are common and disproportionate to nutritional state.
Lymphoproliferation with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly overlaps clinically with autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.
Interstitial lung disease and recurrent respiratory infection may occur, and some patients have hypogammaglobulinaemia despite an autoimmunity-predominant phenotype.
Constitutive STAT3 activation skews T-helper differentiation and reduces regulatory T-cell numbers and function, driving loss of self-tolerance.
JAK inhibitors and interleukin-6 pathway blockade are rational targeted therapies, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used in severe or refractory disease.
reference.pathophysiology: STAT3 is a transcription factor activated by the JAK family downstream of numerous cytokine receptors, including those for interleukin-6, interleukin-10, interleukin-21 and interleukin-23. Heterozygous germline gain-of-function variants render STAT3 hyperactive or constitutively active, increasing transcription of its target genes. This disturbs the balance between effector T-helper responses (particularly the Th17 axis) and regulatory T cells, reduces regulatory T-cell numbers and function partly through interference with interleukin-2 and STAT5 signalling, and promotes survival and expansion of autoreactive lymphocytes. The net effect is early-onset multi-system autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation and impaired immune homeostasis. This contrasts sharply with dominant-negative loss-of-function STAT3 variants, which impair Th17 development and produce the hyper-IgE syndrome phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Common variable immunodeficiency with autoimmune and lymphoproliferative complications
additionalInvestigations: Targeted panel or exome sequencing including STAT3, with functional confirmation such as transactivation reporter or phospho-STAT3 assays
Serum immunoglobulin quantification and specific antibody or vaccine response testing
Lymphocyte immunophenotyping with enumeration of regulatory T cells
Broad autoantibody screen covering islet, thyroid and cytopenia-associated antibodies
Direct antiglobulin test and blood film to characterise autoimmune cytopenias
Thyroid function and glucose or glycated haemoglobin assessment for endocrine autoimmunity
High-resolution chest imaging and nodal/abdominal imaging for interstitial lung disease and lymphoproliferation
redFlags: Multiple simultaneous or sequential autoimmune diseases arising in early childhood
Combination of autoimmune cytopenia with enteropathy and endocrinopathy in one patient
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and often severe, with multi-organ autoimmunity, infection and interstitial lung disease driving morbidity. Targeted JAK or interleukin-6 inhibition and, in refractory cases, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Labelling the illness as an isolated autoimmune disorder (such as type 1 diabetes or immune thrombocytopenia) and missing the unifying monogenic diagnosis.
Confusing STAT3 gain-of-function with STAT3 loss-of-function hyper-IgE syndrome, which have opposite mechanisms and phenotypes.
Assuming normal immunoglobulins exclude the diagnosis, as hypogammaglobulinaemia can coexist.
Attributing short stature solely to chronic illness or corticosteroids rather than the intrinsic disorder.
references: IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
ESID clinical guidance on immune dysregulation disorders
management: Targeted therapy with JAK inhibition and interleukin-6 receptor blockade (tocilizumab) to counter constitutive STAT3 activity
Immunosuppression with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents for autoimmune cytopenias, enteropathy and other organ-specific autoimmunity
Hormone replacement and glycaemic control for early-onset type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease, with nutritional support for failure to thrive
Immunoglobulin replacement and infection prophylaxis where hypogammaglobulinaemia and recurrent respiratory infection occur
Monitor for and manage interstitial lung disease and lymphoproliferation
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in refractory, severe multisystem disease
Genetic counselling for this germline dominant disorder, with family evaluation
